gloss: rock; bind up, shut in, besiege; treat as foe; fashion, form; neck
summary: צוּר is rock: crag, cliff and flint, the hard and lasting stone that water was struck from at Horeb, and above all a name for God, “the Rock, his work is perfect”, beside whom there is no other rock (Deu 32:4; Isa 44:8). The same letters are a verb “bind up, shut in”, used most of an army shutting a city in, with מָצוֹר “siege” and מְצוּרָה “siege-works, stronghold”; a verb “treat as a foe”; a verb “fashion”, with צוּרָה “form” and צִיר “image”; and the noun צַוָּאר “neck”, the neck that bears a yoke. The cognates show more than one older sound behind the צ: the rock has the ṯ̣ of Aramaic טוּר and Ugaritic ġr “mountain” (Daniel’s mountain, Dan 2:35), while “bind” and “form” have the plain ṣ of Aramaic צוּר and Arabic ṣawwara.

senses.definition: A mass of hard stone in the open: a crag to climb or hide in, a cliff with clefts, a rock to offer on or engrave in. It stands for what is hard, high and lasting.

evidence.note: “I will stand before you there on the צוּר in Horeb, and you shall strike the צוּר, and water shall come out of it.”
“I will put you in a cleft of the צוּר and cover you with my hand.”
Words engraved with an iron pen and lead “in the צוּר for ever”: the rock as what lasts.
“The צוּר is moved from its place”: what does not move, moved.
“From the top of צֻרִים I see him, and from the hills I behold him.”
“Enter into the צוּר and hide in the dust from the terror of Yahweh” (and 2:19, 21).
Fire rose from the צוּר and consumed Gideon’s offering.
Manoah offered the kid on the צוּר to Yahweh.
Oreb slain at צוּר־עוֹרֵב, the rock of Oreb (Isa 10:26).
Saul sought David on the צוּרֵי of the wild goats.
Rizpah spread sackcloth for herself on the צוּר.
“He will set me up on a צוּר.”
“Lead me to the צוּר that is higher than I.”
The way of a serpent on a צוּר.
The miner cuts channels in the צוּרוֹת.
“The צֻרִים are broken down by him.”
Three of the thirty went down to the צֻר to David, to the cave of Adullam.

senses.definition: The rock in the wilderness from which Yahweh gave Israel water, struck at Horeb (Exo 17:6) and remembered in the psalms and prophets; with it, rock that yields honey and oil, the land’s plenty from the hardest place.

evidence.note: “He split צֻרִים in the wilderness and gave them drink as from the great depths” (and 78:20).
“He opened the צוּר and waters gushed out.”
He turns the צוּר into a pool of water.
“He made water flow from the צוּר for them; he split the צוּר.”
Who brought you water out of the צוּר of flint.
Honey from the סֶלַע and oil from the flinty צוּר.
“With honey from the צוּר I would satisfy you.”
“The צוּר poured out for me streams of oil.”
“They drank from the spiritual rock (πέτρα) that followed them, and the rock was Christ.”

senses.definition: Rock as hard, sharp stone: flint knives, and the edge of a sword.

evidence.note: “Make for yourself חַרְבוֹת צֻרִים”, knives of flint, and circumcise Israel again.
“You have turned back the צוּר of his sword”: its edge.

senses.definition: Figuratively, the rock from which a people is cut: its forefather.

evidence.note: “Look to the צוּר you were hewn from … look to Abraham your father and to Sarah who bore you” (51:1–2).

senses.definition: A name for God: the one who does not move or fail, in whom his people take refuge, who saves them and is faithful to them; set beside fortress, high tower, shield and salvation. The gods of the nations are called their “rock” only to be set against him.

evidence.note: “The צוּר, his work is perfect, for all his ways are justice; a God of faithfulness and without injustice, righteous and upright is he.”
“Who is God (אֵל) except Yahweh, and who is a צוּר except our God?” (Psa 18:32).
“Is there a God besides me? There is no צוּר; I know not any.”
“There is none holy like Yahweh, for there is none besides you, and there is no צוּר like our God.”
“Yahweh is my סֶלַע and my fortress and my deliverer; my God, my צוּר, I take refuge in him.”
Jeshurun grew fat and “scorned the צוּר of his salvation”.
“The צוּר who begot you you neglected, and forgot the God who gave you birth.”
“Unless their צוּר had sold them.”
“Their צוּר is not as our צוּר”: the nations’ gods set against Israel’s God.
“Where are their gods, the צוּר in whom they took refuge?”
“The God of Israel said, the צוּר of Israel spoke to me.”
To come to the mountain of Yahweh, to the צוּר of Israel.
“Trust in Yahweh for ever, for in יָהּ יַהְוֶה is an everlasting צוּר (צוּר עוֹלָמִים).”
“You have forgotten the God of your salvation and have not remembered the צוּר of your strength.”
Yahweh of armies will be a sanctuary, and “a stone of stumbling and a צוּר of offence” to both houses of Israel.
“Yahweh, my צוּר and my redeemer.”
“Be to me a צוּר of strength, a house of fortresses to save me.”
“He alone is my צוּר and my salvation, my high tower; I shall not be greatly moved” (and 62:7–8).
“My flesh and my heart fail, but God is the צוּר of my heart and my portion for ever.”
They remembered that God was their צוּר, and the Most High God their redeemer.
David’s son “shall cry to me, You are my father, my God, and the צוּר of my salvation.”
“Yahweh is upright; my צוּר, and there is no unrighteousness in him.”
“Let us shout aloud to the צוּר of our salvation.”
“Blessed be Yahweh my צוּר, who trains my hands for war.”
“O צוּר, you have established him for correction.”

evidence.locator: Exo.17.6, צּוּר → πέτρας, πέτραν; Isa.8.14, צוּר → πέτρα; Psa.78.15, צֻרִים → πέτρα; Isa.48.21; Isa.51.1
evidence.note: The Septuagint’s commonest Greek for the rock; for God as the Rock it mostly puts θεός (Deu.32.4, 18, 31).
The rock of Exo 17:6 and the psalms: “and the rock was Christ.”
Isa 8:14 with 28:16: “a stone of stumbling and a rock (πέτρα) of offence”.
Isa 8:14 again, of Jesus, rejected by the builders.

parallels.note: Cliff, crag: the other word for rock, beside צוּר in the same line.

evidence.note: He split צֻרִים (78:15); he brought streams out of the סֶלַע (78:16).

parallels.note: Fortress: the rock as the place one is safe in.
High tower, refuge on a height.
The Rock is “the rock of my salvation”: what he is, he is to save.
God and Rock as one: who is God, who is a rock, but Yahweh.

words.summary: A hollow verb, beside the doubled צָרַר “bind, be narrow, be hostile”, with which it shares forms and part of its meaning: what this verb’s cognate Aramaic צוּר means is “tie around”. Most often it is an army shutting a city in (צוּר עַל), the siege the nouns מָצוֹר and מְצוּרָה name.

stems.gloss: bind up; shut in, enclose; besiege

senses.gloss: bind up, tie in a bundle
senses.definition: To tie up something, silver above all, in a bag or the hand, to carry it.

evidence.note: Turn the tithe into silver, “and bind up (וְצַרְתָּ) the silver in your hand”, and go to the place Yahweh will choose.
Naaman “bound two talents of silver in two bags”.
The king’s scribe and the high priest “bound up and counted” the silver found in Yahweh’s house.
Take a few of the hairs “and bind them in your skirts”.

senses.definition: To close something in on every side.

evidence.note: “Behind and before צַרְתָּנִי, you have shut me in, and laid your hand on me.”
“If she is a door, we will enclose her (נָצוּר עָלֶיהָ) with boards of cedar.”

senses.definition: Of an army, to shut a city in: to camp around it and cut it off until it is taken or starved. Usually צוּר עַל, sometimes אֶל or with a direct object.

evidence.note: “If it will not make peace with you but makes war against you, then you shall besiege it.”
“When you besiege a city many days, making war against it to take it, you shall not destroy its trees.”
Ben-hadad went up “and besieged Samaria”, and there was a great famine while they besieged it (6:25).
The king of Assyria besieged Samaria three years.
Rezin and Pekah besieged Ahaz, but could not prevail.
Nebuchadnezzar’s servants were besieging Jerusalem.
In Jehoiakim’s third year Nebuchadnezzar came to Jerusalem “and besieged it”.
In Zedekiah’s ninth year, the tenth month, Babylon’s army came and besieged Jerusalem.
The Chaldeans besieging Jerusalem withdrew at news of Pharaoh’s army.
“The Chaldeans who besiege you outside the wall.”
Whoever goes out and falls to the Chaldeans who besiege you will live.
Yahweh against Ariel: “I will camp against you round about, and lay siege against you with a mound, and raise siege-works (מְצֻרֹת) against you.”
The prophet acts out the siege: “it shall be in siege (בַמָּצוֹר), and you shall besiege it; a sign to the house of Israel.”
“Go up, Elam! Besiege (צוּרִי), Media!”
Saul summoned the people to go down to Keilah “to besiege David and his men”.
Joab and Israel destroyed Ammon and besieged Rabbah (1Ch 20:1).
They besieged Sheba in Abel of Beth-maacah and cast up a mound against the city.
Nadab and all Israel were besieging Gibbethon.
“If his enemy besieges him in the land of his gates” (2Ch 6:28): one of the troubles Solomon prays over.

parallels.note: Camp against a city: the siege begins with the camp around it.
Fight against: the siege is the war’s means of taking the city.

words.summary: The neck, mostly in the plural for a single neck: where one falls in embrace, wears a chain, bears a yoke, or stiffens in pride. Its tie to the root’s senses is not clear; the noun has its own cognates in Aramaic and, perhaps, Arabic “incline the neck”.

senses.definition: The neck of man or beast: fallen on in embrace and weeping, adorned with chains, trodden on by a conqueror.

evidence.note: Esau ran to meet Jacob, embraced him, “and fell on his neck (צַוָּארָו) and kissed him”.
Joseph fell on Benjamin’s neck and wept, and Benjamin wept on his neck.
Joseph fell on Israel’s neck “and wept on his neck a long while”.
Pharaoh put a chain of gold on Joseph’s neck.
Rebekah put the kid skins on the smooth of Jacob’s neck.
The crescent ornaments on the camels’ necks (and 8:26).
“Your neck with strings of jewels.”
“Your neck is like the tower of David” (and 7:5, a tower of ivory).
The war horse: “Do you clothe his neck with a mane?”
“In his neck strength lodges.”
“Put your feet on the necks of these kings”: the conquered under the conqueror’s foot.
To lay you on the necks of the slain.

senses.definition: The neck as what bears a yoke: to put one’s neck under it is to serve, to break it from the neck is to be set free.

evidence.note: “You shall serve your brother; and when you break loose, you shall break his yoke from your neck.”
“He will put a yoke of iron on your neck until he has destroyed you.”
The nation “that will not put its neck under the yoke of the king of Babylon” (and 27:11–12, bring your neck under the yoke and live).
Hananiah took the yoke from Jeremiah’s neck and broke it; Yahweh answers with an iron yoke on the neck of all these nations (28:14).
“I will break his yoke from your neck, and strangers shall no more make him serve.”
Assyria’s yoke taken from your neck.
“Loose yourself from the bands of your neck, captive daughter of Zion.”
The yoke of my transgressions has come up on my neck.
“On our necks we are pursued.”
Ephraim a trained heifer: “I passed over her fair neck”, to put her under the yoke.
An evil from which you shall not remove your necks.
“Why do you put a yoke on the neck of the disciples, which neither our fathers nor we could bear?”

senses.definition: The neck held up against God or refused to a task.

evidence.note: “Do not lift up your horn on high; do not speak with a stiff neck (בְצַוָּאר עָתָק).”
The wicked runs against God “with a neck”, with the thick bosses of his shields.
The nobles of Tekoa “did not put their neck (צַוָּרָם) to the work of their Lord”.

senses.definition: As a measure: a flood that reaches the neck leaves only the head above it.

evidence.note: Assyria will sweep into Judah, overflow and pass through, “it will reach to the neck”.
His breath like an overflowing stream that reaches to the neck.
Laying bare the foundation to the neck.

evidence.locator: Gen.33.4, צַוָּאר → τράχηλον; Gen.45.14; Gen.46.29; Jer.27.8, צַוָּאר → τράχηλον

evidence.note: The father ran and fell on his son’s neck and kissed him, as Esau and Joseph did.
The yoke on the neck.
The Ephesian elders fell on Paul’s neck.
Priscilla and Aquila laid down their own necks for Paul’s life.

words.summary: What צוּר “besiege” does: the state of a city shut in, the works raised to shut it in, and, from the other side, the fortification that holds out against them. Deuteronomy’s curse of siege (Deu 28:52–57) is quoted by Jeremiah and acted out by Ezekiel.

senses.definition: A city’s being shut in by an enemy, and the time it lasts, with its hunger and thirst.

evidence.note: “You shall eat the fruit of your own body … in the siege and in the distress (בְּמָצוֹר וּבְמָצוֹק) with which your enemies shall distress you” (and 28:55, 57).
“The city came into siege (בַּמָּצוֹר) until the eleventh year of king Zedekiah”; then the famine prevailed (25:3).
Nebuchadnezzar’s servants came up to Jerusalem, and the city came into siege.
Jeremiah takes up Deu 28:53: they shall eat the flesh of their sons and daughters “in the siege and in the distress”.
“Gather up your bundle from the land, you who dwell in the siege.”
“Set your face toward the siege of Jerusalem” (and 4:8; 5:2, when the days of the siege are fulfilled).
To Nineveh: “Draw water for the siege; strengthen your forts.”
“He has laid siege against us; they strike the judge of Israel with a rod on the cheek.”
Jerusalem a cup of reeling to the peoples round about, “and against Judah also it shall be in the siege against Jerusalem”.
Sennacherib: “On what do you trust, that you abide in the siege in Jerusalem?”

senses.definition: What a besieger builds against a city to take it.

evidence.note: Only trees not for food you may cut down “and build siege-works (מָצוֹר) against the city that makes war with you, until it falls”.
The tree of the field is not a man, to go before you into the siege.
“Lay siege (מָצוֹר) against it, build a siege wall against it, cast up a mound against it.”

senses.definition: The defence a city builds to stand a siege: rampart and walls, and a fortified city.

evidence.note: “Tyre built herself a stronghold (מָצוֹר) and heaped up silver like dust.”
Solomon built Beth-horon, “fortified cities (עָרֵי מָצוֹר), with walls, gates and bars”.
Rehoboam built cities “for defence (לְמָצוֹר) in Judah”.
“He has shown me his marvellous kindness in a fortified city (בְּעִיר מָצוֹר).”
“Who will bring me into the fortified city?”
“I will stand on my watch and station myself on the rampart (מָצוֹר).”

evidence.locator: Deu.28.53, מָצוֹר → στενοχωρίᾳ (also 28:55, 57); Deu.20.20, מָצוֹר → χαράκωσιν; Ezk.4.2, מָצוֹר → περιοχήν

evidence.note: “Shall tribulation or distress (στενοχωρία) … separate us from the love of Christ?”

words.summary: Like מָצוֹר: what is raised against a city, and what a city raises to hold out. Mostly in Chronicles’ עָרֵי מְצֻרוֹת, “fortified cities”.

senses.definition: Works raised against a besieged city.

evidence.note: “I will lay siege against you with a mound and raise מְצֻרֹת against you.”

senses.definition: A place made strong to stand a siege; with עָרֵי, fortified cities.

evidence.note: Rehoboam “strengthened the strongholds (הַמְּצֻרוֹת) and put commanders in them, and stores of food, oil and wine”.
Zorah, Aijalon and Hebron, “fortified cities (עָרֵי מְצֻרוֹת) in Judah and Benjamin”.
Shishak took the fortified cities of Judah and came to Jerusalem.
“Guard the rampart (נָצוֹר מְצֻרָה), watch the way, strengthen your loins.”

words.summary: A few times צוּר is “be an adversary to”, set beside אָיַב “be an enemy”. It means what the doubled צָרַר “be hostile” means (whose participle צֹרֵר is “adversary”, Num 10:9), and may be a by-form of it. Its tie to “bind, besiege” is not clear; Arabic ḍāra “harm” is a possible cognate, with another older sound behind the צ.

senses.definition: To act as an enemy toward someone: to provoke, oppose or attack.

evidence.note: “I will be an enemy to your enemies (וְאָיַבְתִּי אֶת־אֹיְבֶיךָ) and an adversary to your adversaries (וְצַרְתִּי אֶת־צֹרְרֶיךָ).”
“Do not harass Moab (אַל־תָּצַר), and do not contend with them in battle.”
The same of Ammon: “do not harass them”.
The Jews may destroy every force “that would assault them (הַצָּרִים אֹתָם)”.
Gaal and his brothers “are stirring up the city against you” (צָרִים אֶת־הָעִיר עָלֶיךָ): making it hostile, or shutting it against Abimelech.
“When you go to war in your land against the adversary who oppresses you (הַצַּר הַצֹּרֵר אֶתְכֶם), blow an alarm with the trumpets”: the doubled form צָרַר, with the same meaning.

words.summary: A verb “fashion, give shape to”, seldom used in Hebrew but common in Aramaic (“draw, shape”) and Arabic (ṣawwara “form, picture”), from which come צוּרָה “form” and צִיר “image”. Its few uses are close to יָצַר “form”.

senses.definition: To give a thing its shape, as a craftsman casts bronze.

evidence.note: Hiram “fashioned (וַיָּצַר) the two pillars of bronze, eighteen cubits high”.
Aaron “fashioned it (וַיָּצַר אֹתוֹ) with a graving tool and made it a molten calf”; the corpus reads the form as יָצַר “form”.

words.summary: The form or design of a thing: in scripture only the form of the house shown to Ezekiel, set beside its ordinances and laws.

senses.definition: The whole shape and arrangement of a building, made known so that it may be kept and done.

evidence.note: “Make known to them the צוּרַת of the house, its arrangement, its exits and entrances, all its צוּרֹתָו and all its ordinances … and write it in their sight, that they may keep all its צוּרָתוֹ and all its ordinances, and do them.”

words.summary: A thing given shape: an idol, and perhaps a body’s form. Two uses only.

senses.definition: A fashioned image of a god.

evidence.note: “They are ashamed and confounded, all of them; the makers of צִירִים go into confusion together.”
“Their form is for the grave (שְׁאוֹל) to wear away”: the written text has וצירם, the read text וְצוּרָם.

words.summary: An ornament of the neck, from צַוָּאר; once, in the plural.

senses.definition: A chain or string worn on the neck.

evidence.note: “You have ravished my heart with one of your eyes, with one chain (עֲנָק) of your necklaces (מִצַּוְּרֹנָיִךְ).”

words.summary: Scripture’s Aramaic for “mountain”: the same word as Hebrew צוּר, with the ט Aramaic writes where Hebrew writes צ for the older ṯ̣ (Ugaritic has ġ, in ġr “mountain”). In Daniel 2 the stone cut from the mountain becomes a mountain that fills the earth.

senses.definition: A mountain: the one the stone was cut from, and the great one it became.

evidence.note: “You saw that a stone was cut out of the mountain (מִטּוּרָא) without hands, and it broke in pieces the iron, the bronze, the clay, the silver and the gold.”
“The stone that struck the image became a great mountain (לְטוּר רַב) and filled the whole earth.”

words.summary: Scripture’s Aramaic for “neck”, as the Hebrew: the neck that wears the gold chain of honour.

senses.definition: The neck, on which a king’s chain of gold is hung.

evidence.note: They clothed Daniel in purple “and put a chain of gold on his neck (עַל־צַוְּארֵהּ)”.
Belshazzar’s promise to whoever reads the writing (and 5:16).

words.summary: The Peshitta’s ܨܘܪܐ (ṣawrā), for τράχηλος: the neck fallen on in embrace, hung with a millstone, put under a yoke.

senses.definition: The neck, in embrace, under a yoke, and laid down for another’s life.

evidence.note: His father ran “and fell on his neck (ܨܘܪܗ) and kissed him”, as in Gen 33:4 and 46:29.
“Why do you put a yoke on the necks of the disciples?”
Better that a millstone be hung on his neck (and Mrk 9:42; Luk 17:2).
“Who gave their necks for my life.”

words.summary: The Peshitta’s ܨܪ (ṣār), “portray, form”, as Aramaic צוּר “draw, shape”: Christ portrayed before the Galatians, and formed in them.

senses.definition: To set out a figure plainly before the eyes.

evidence.note: “Jesus the Messiah was as if portrayed (ܨܝܪ) before your eyes when he was crucified.”

senses.definition: To take shape, of Christ in believers.

evidence.note: “My children, for whom I am in labour again until the Messiah is formed (ܕܢܬܬܨܝܪ) in you.”

words.summary: The Peshitta’s ܨܘܪܬܐ (ṣūrtā), “image, portrayal”, as Aramaic צוּרְתָא and Hebrew צוּרָה.

senses.definition: The image or form of someone, to which others are made like.

evidence.note: “He knew them beforehand and marked them out in the likeness of the image (ܕܨܘܪܬܐ) of his Son, that he might be the firstborn of many brothers.”

cognates.gloss: a hard stone with a sharp edge, used as a knife
cognates.note: The rock as hard, sharp stone, as in Joshua’s flint knives (Jos 5:2). Arabic ẓ answers to the older ṯ̣, which Hebrew writes צ and Aramaic ט.

evidence.note: A sharp-edged hard stone; he cut off a sharp-edged fragment of hard stone

cognates.note: The same word as צוּר and Aramaic טוּר: Ugaritic ġ for the older ṯ̣.
The Targums’ word for “mountain”, as Daniel’s טוּר.

evidence.note: mount, mountain; Targ. O. Exo 3:12

cognates.note: Hard, sharp stone, as צוּר in “knives of flint” (Jos 5:2). Akkadian ṣ does not show which older sound stands behind it.

evidence.note: flint; obsidian

cognates.note: The binding sense of the verb, as in “bind up the silver” (Deu 14:25).

evidence.note: to tie around: coins tied up in a sheet, a cloak tied up

cognates.gloss: draw, shape, design; form, figure, painting

evidence.note: to draw, shape, design
= Hebrew צוּרָה; Targ. O. Deu 4:16

cognates.gloss: he formed, fashioned, shaped, pictured; form, figure, shape
cognates.note: The participle مُصَوِّرٌ, “the Fashioner”, is used of God as the one who gives each thing its form.

evidence.note: He formed, fashioned, figured, shaped, sculptured, or pictured
Form, fashion, figure, shape; the Former, or Fashioner

cognates.gloss: drawing, design, ground-plan; ordinances; draw, design
cognates.note: Strikingly close to Ezekiel’s צוּרָה of the house beside its ordinances, but the Akkadian root is ʾṣr, which may rather answer to יָצַר “form”.

evidence.note: design; drawing; ground-plan; (divine) plan; ordinances
Targ. Isa 3:16; Targ. Y. Gen 45:14; “up to their necks”

cognates.gloss: make to incline (said especially of the neck); having a bent neck
cognates.note: The Arabic root of “form” is also used of inclining the neck; whether this bears on צַוָּאר is uncertain.

evidence.note: He made it, or specially the neck, to incline
A man having an inclining, or a bending, or crooked, neck

cognates.note: With ḍarra “harm”, the Arabic of the doubled צָרַר “be hostile”. It would put the older ṣ́ behind the צ of “treat as a foe”, and so another root than “bind” and “rock”.

evidence.note: It harmed, injured, hurt him; as also ضَارَهُ, aor. يَضُورُ

doctrine.statement: Yahweh calls himself the Rock and says there is no other: “Is there a God besides me? There is no Rock; I know not any” (Isa 44:8). Hannah and David say the same: there is no rock like our God, and who is a rock except our God (1Sa 2:2; 2Sa 22:32). The Rock’s work is perfect and he is faithful (Deu 32:4); he begot Israel (Deu 32:18); the nations’ gods are called their rock only to be denied the name, “their rock is not as our Rock” (Deu 32:31, 37). So the name belongs to the one God alone, and what it says of him is that he does not move or fail, and that those who take refuge in him are saved (Psa 18:3; 62:3, 7).

At Horeb Yahweh stood on the rock and Moses struck it, and water came out of it for the people (Exo 17:6). Paul says of that rock, “the rock was Christ” (1Co 10:4): the son is the rock that was struck, through whom God gives the water of life, as Jesus himself offered it (Joh 7:37–39). Yahweh of armies says he will be “a rock of stumbling” to both houses of Israel (Isa 8:14), and Paul and Peter apply the words to Jesus, the stone God lays in Zion (Rom 9:33; 1Pe 2:6–8). The Rock remains the one God (Isa 44:8); Christ is the rock God provided and laid, and the son of David calls God “my father, my God, and the rock of my salvation” (Psa 89:27).

In Nebuchadnezzar’s dream a stone cut out of the mountain (טוּר) without hands strikes the image of the kingdoms of men, and becomes a great mountain that fills the whole earth (Dan 2:34–35, 45). Daniel explains it: the God of heaven will set up a kingdom that will never be destroyed; it will break in pieces all these kingdoms and stand for ever (Dan 2:44). Jesus speaks of himself as that stone, which grinds to powder whoever it falls on (Luk 20:17–18). The kingdom of God is therefore a kingdom on the earth, filling it in place of the kingdoms of men, set up by God and not by human hands.

Moses warned that if Israel would not obey, an enemy would besiege them in all their gates until their high walls came down, and in the siege they would eat their own children (Deu 28:52–57). It came on Samaria (2Ki 6:24–29) and on Jerusalem when Babylon besieged it from Zedekiah’s ninth year to his eleventh, until the famine prevailed (2Ki 25:1–3; Lam 4:10); Jeremiah repeats Moses’ words, “in the siege and in the distress” (Jer 19:9), and Ezekiel acts the siege out as a sign to the house of Israel (Ezk 4:1–3). Jesus foretold it once more: “your enemies will cast up a rampart around you and hem you in on every side” (Luk 19:43–44), and “when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies, know that its desolation has come near” (Luk 21:20). That siege came when Rome took Jerusalem and destroyed the temple in AD 70, the second time the covenant’s curse of siege fell on the city.

The Peshitta uses this root for what God does in those he calls: they are marked out “in the likeness of the image (ܨܘܪܬܐ) of his Son” (Rom 8:29), and Paul labours “until the Messiah is formed (ܢܬܬܨܝܪ) in you” (Gal 4:19), having first set him out before their eyes “as if portrayed” on the cross (Gal 3:1). As the house in Ezekiel had a form to be kept and done (Ezk 43:11), the believer has a form to be shaped to: the crucified son.

note: Root key צור, as the corpus keys it. BDB files four verbs and the nouns under צור: r.bk.aa (bind, besiege) with r.bk.ab מָצוֹר and r.bk.ac מְצוּרָה; r.bl.aa (treat as foe); r.bm.aa (fashion) with r.bm.ab צוּרָה and r.bm.ac צִיר; r.bn.ab צוּר rock; r.bj.ab צַוָּאר and r.bj.ac צַוָּרוֹן. Cross-reference keys with no tokens are put on their words: m.dc.ak (מָצוֹר) on מָצוֹר, m.df.ae (מְצֻרָה) on מְצוּרָה, r.aw.ae and r.bn.ag (צַוָּר, Neh 3:5) on צַוָּאר. Left out: the proper names צוּר Zur (r.bn.ac: a Midianite prince, Num 25:15; 31:8; Jos 13:21; and a Benjamite, 1Ch 8:30; 9:36) and צוּרִיאֵל Zuriel (r.bn.ad, Num 3:35) have no name entries yet; צוּרִישַׁדָּי and אֱלִיצוּר have theirs, and פְּדָהצוּר is under פדה. Tyre צֹר (r.dr.an) and Beth-zur are places; מָצוֹר “Egypt” (m.df.ac, Mic 7:12 etc.) belongs to מצר though the corpus tags Mic 7:12 here. Flint צֹר (Exo 4:25; Ezk 3:9; r.eb.ac) BDB files under צרר; it is surely the same word as צוּר “flint” (Jos 5:2) and might be moved here when צרר is written. The corpus analyses many doubled צָרַר forms as this root (צֹרֵר “adversary”, צְרוּרָה, צַר־לִי “I am in distress”, the hiphil הֵצַר, מְצֵרָה “woman in labour”, Jos 9:4 מְצֹרָרִים, Isa 8:16 צוֹר “bind up the testimony”) and its surfaces carry r.bk.aa beside the צרר keys, so lexicon-support’s count of uses for r.bk.aa includes them. They are left to a צרר entry; Num 10:9 is cited under צוּר II only for its shared meaning. 1Ki 8:37 = 2Ch 6:28 יָצַר and 2Ch 28:20 וַיָּצַר are tagged hiphil by the corpus; the first is read here as qal “besiege”, the second (“distressed him and did not strengthen him”) is left to צרר. Exo 32:4 is read by the corpus as יָצַר. Psa 49:15 Kethiv וצירם / Qere וְצוּרָם carries no key. The Peshitta’s ܛܘܪܐ “mountain” (very common in the Gospels) is not added as a word; it answers to Hebrew הַר as much as to צוּר. Greek: Luk 19:43 χάραξ, the rampart of the siege, is near the Septuagint’s χαράκωσις for מָצוֹר (Deu 20:20) but not the same word. The ar-dara cognate is a lead only; צוּר II may be no more than a by-form of צרר. Lane p. 1744 also has صَارَةٌ “the top of a mountain” under صور (n25177), with ṣ: not followed, since the rock’s cognates show ṯ̣.
